subtopic: Telling the truth after a mistake
subtype: Approach: fixing the harm along with the apology [Action]
passage: My name is Kashish, and this is about the day I spilled water on Zubin's drawing of a lighthouse. He had worked on it for a week. The blue sea ran into the sky. I said sorry right away, and Zubin nodded, but sorry did not bring the lighthouse back. So after school I asked to borrow the pencil sketch, and I redrew the lighthouse slowly on a clean sheet, following his outline. It took two evenings, and mine leaned a little. When I gave it back Zubin looked at it for a long time and said, "It leans. But thanks." I still think that was the right thing to do.

qa.q: What did Kashish spill on Zubin's drawing?
What did Kashish feel about saying sorry alone?
qa.a: Kashish felt it did not fix the loss and wanted to make it right, so the lighthouse was redrawn.

qa.q: What could Kashish do if the second drawing still disappoints Zubin?
qa.a: Ask what would help and offer to redo the coloured parts together, because repair means listening to the person who lost the work.

qa.q: How might Zubin see the redrawn lighthouse?
qa.a: As a kind effort even though it leans, since Zubin looked at it a long time and said thanks.

grounding: Kashish says sorry and also redraws the spoiled drawing, so repair goes beyond words.

passage:
Art room note, Thursday.
During the painting lesson, Sangeeta knocked her water jar across Priya's finished drawing of a peacock. Priya burst into tears. Sangeeta said "Sorry" at once, but I could see that saying it didn't satisfy her. She asked if she could stay back at lunch. For forty minutes she sat with a fresh sheet and Priya's smudged drawing beside it, copying the peacock's outline carefully, then asked Priya to come and colour it with her. When Priya arrived, the outline was ready and neat. They painted the feathers together. Sangeeta told me, "Sorry doesn't give her the drawing back. This does." I have put both drawings, the smudged one and the new one, on the class board.
Dilnaz, art teacher

qa.q: Why wasn't saying sorry enough for Sangeeta?
qa.a: She felt guilty and knew that words alone would not give Priya her drawing back.

qa.q: What else could Sangeeta have done if there was no time at lunch?
qa.a: Offered to redraw it at home and bring it the next day, still repairing the harm.

qa.q: How might Priya feel arriving at lunch?
qa.a: Surprised and comforted to find the outline ready and a friend to paint with.

grounding: An art teacher's note records a girl who spoiled a classmate's drawing apologising and redrawing it, seeing repair as more than words.

passage:
Wednesday
Today I spoilt Simran's drawing for the competition. I leaned on it with my elbow while it was still wet, and the whole sky smudged into the mountains. Simran didn't cry, but she went very quiet, and that was worse. I said sorry about five times. It didn't feel like enough. Sorry doesn't fix a sky. So after school I asked Simran if I could borrow her pencil sketch, and at home I redrew the mountains exactly the same size on new paper, very carefully, using a ruler for the lake. Tomorrow I'll give it to her so she only has to paint it. Mummy said, "That's a real sorry." I hope Simran thinks so too.
Shreya

qa.q: What did Shreya lean on the drawing with?
How did Shreya feel when Simran went quiet?
qa.a: Shreya felt guilty, and the silence felt worse than tears.

qa.q: What else could Shreya do tomorrow?
qa.a: Shreya could offer to help paint or ask the teacher for extra time, so Simran is not rushed.

qa.q: How might Simran feel receiving the redrawn sketch?
qa.a: Simran may feel relieved and cared for, seeing Shreya took real trouble to fix it.

grounding: A diary entry shows a child who spoiled a classmate's drawing apologising and redrawing it, understanding repair matters more than words.
